posts.name: Vishal Gupta
posts.cooked:
Hi Experts,

I am very new to the world of Linux. I plan to build a virtualization platform on Ubuntu and searched about the two options that I have i.e. Ubuntu Pro and Ubuntu LTS. I have a single workstation with 64GB RAM and 1TB SSD where I intend to install VMs for testing various tools from time to time on different OS platforms. Even though I read through the comments and other material that is available on the licensing for Pro, I still have some questions. I have listed them below and if someone can provide some clarity, it will help me in making the right choice to build my lab environment.

  1. Let’s say I install Ubuntu Pro for a personal lab and have may be 2 - 3 VMs (for a DC and a couple other common services) always on with other VMs that just utilize these resources, from time to time. If I have just one or two other VMs switched on and other VMs are offline, do those offline VMs still count against the licensed number limit of 5 VMs?
  2. In the same scenario as above, if I have more than 5 VMs switched on but do not have the Pro token attached to more than 5 VMs, will this be considered a violation of license terms?
  3. Is it compulsory for me to attach the Pro token to all the VMs that I am running in KVM, if I use Ubuntu Pro?

Now for a more general query: I have seen multiple replies in this post where it was advised that it is being considered whether the number of VMs for personal use can be increased, but as per documentation and what is advertised, it still seems to be restricted to 5 VMs. I am trying to learn various different technologies including Linux and could really use a stable environment to work in. Is this number expected to change anytime soon?

posts.name: Charles L. Nix, II
posts.cooked: This has literally been asked and answered dozens of times. As I understand, for personal use, 5 physical machines, unlimited VMs. And that’s 5 physical machines withing 24 hours. Search many answers, particularly from @Lech and you can confirm for yourself.

To be honest, for me it is still not clear either.

Does it mean:
You can install Ubuntu on five physical machines, activate Ubuntu Pro on those five machines and then install unlimited VMs via KVM on those five machines, but not activate Ubuntu pro in those VMs

Or does it mean:
You can run any Hypervisor on five physical Machines, install unlimited VMs of Ubuntu on those five physical machines and activate Ubuntu Pro on all those Ubuntu VMs running on the five physical Machines no matter if they in sum are more then five VMs.

posts.name: Vishal Gupta
posts.cooked: I read through the threads again and some of it got answered, Thanks, Charles. One of my questions which is pertaining to pro attaching VMs and if that will add to the licensing count in my Ubuntu Pro subscription, is still unanswered though. I see multiple mentions of being able to run unlimited VMs on a Pro activated host but did not find any thread discussing activating Pro on VMs and if that consumes licensing too. Maybe I missed a thread where this is answered, and you could point me to it?

posts.name: Ian Weisser
posts.cooked:
linxnoob:

I see multiple mentions of being able to run unlimited VMs on a Pro activated host but did not find any thread discussing activating Pro on VMs and if that consumes licensing too.

Let’s try it this way:

  • If you use Pro only on the bare-metal VM host system, that’s a single Pro instance. None of the VMs count toward your limit.

    This is a common use case, and this is perhaps what you read elsewhere. None of the VM guests get the benefits of Pro…but many VMs don’t need those benefits anyway.

  • If you use Pro on both the host and VM guests, then each counts toward your limit.

    Not ALL your VMs. Just the host and each active VM with Pro installed.

posts.name: Vishal Gupta
posts.cooked: That’s the information that I was looking for. Thanks Ian!

posts.name: Marcus Bainbridge
posts.cooked:
I’ve read through all the replies here and I’m even more confused about the Pro license options.

I work for a large enterprise, and run Ubuntu Desktop on a Hyper-V server (since I don’t have enough storage on my laptop to do what I want). Our corporate security scanners regularly complain that I don’t have the ESM patches, so I’m looking at a Pro subscription.

Technically, I’m only using it for personal use, but it all depends on how “Personal use” is defined. I’m using it to evaluate a microprocessor, and the dev environment for it requires Ubuntu. I’m not using it to develop a commercial product. Also, the “Ubuntu Pro Personal terms” states that only one account per company is allowed, which conflicts with the headline statement: “Free, personal subscription for 5 machines for you or any business you own”. (my highlighting)

On the purchase options, it gets more confusing. The server option now relates to “Physical servers”, not a stand-alone VM running on a server.

Hence my confusion. Can I use a free license, or if not, do I need a Desktop or Server license?

posts.name: Oliver Grawert
posts.cooked:
mbainbridge:

only one account per company is allowed, which conflicts with the headline statement: “Free, personal subscription for 5 machines

Your free account will have five tokens you can use to your liking on different systems so there is no contradiction here … (I can’t talk about the commercial side though, someone else will have to chime in for this but I thought I might be able to help with the confusion )

posts.name: Graham Lucking
posts.cooked:
@mbainbridge

I do not see how you can claim that your work is for personal use when you are working for the benefit of an employer and doing so during time paid for by your employer.

When we set up a Ubuntu pro account/subscription we indicate whether we are a personal user or an enterprise user.

As an individual user I have never investigated what happens when I click Enterprise. But surely that is the option that you would honestly choose.

I also think that your employer should take responsibility for this. Perhaps someone with authority could make use of the Chatbot.

I also wonder why you would need ESM if you are using a version of Ubuntu still in life support.

By the way, in my opinion, if you do set up a Ubuntu Pro subscription it will not cover the Hyper-V machine only the installation of Ubuntu running in the VM.

Regards

posts.name: colin h winter
posts.cooked:
The answer above (post 23) says “critical vulnerabilities are released within 24 hours”, across every supported release. Since June, 57 kernel CVEs in ubuntu-cve-tracker were raised from medium to critical on their Ubuntu CVSS v4 score (“Priority reason: See ubuntu cvss score”). Of the 24 fixed after being raised, none was fixed within a week, at a median of 16.5 days; 9 more were still waiting on 20 October. The tracker commit, fix date and release status for each one, with the scripts: https://markovianprotocol.com/measurements/sm-023.html?r=ubuntufaq

Three questions, which we’ll print with your answers: does the 24-hour line cover kernel CVEs raised to critical from the CVSS score, and if not, will the FAQ or the label change? Under the two-week kernel cycle announced on 23 September, what should users expect for those? And for the 14 that are fixed on some supported releases but still needed on others, is there a date?
